html:
The Banana massacre was the killing of striking workers of the United Fruit Company by the Colombian army in the town of Ciénaga on 6 December 1928. The number of dead is unknown; estimates range from dozens to many hundreds.

Thousands of banana workers on the Caribbean coast had struck for weeks, demanding contracts, pay in money instead of company vouchers, and an eight-hour day. The United Fruit Company and the US government pressed the government to act. Troops opened fire on a crowd gathered in the town square.

The young lawyer Jorge Eliécer Gaitán made his name investigating the killings in Congress. García Márquez put the massacre at the heart of One Hundred Years of Solitude. It became a symbol of the banana republics across Colombia and Latin America.
